narrative: Based on your application details, the model has predicted a 99.2% probability that you would not pass the bar exam on your first attempt, which unfortunately led to the rejection of your university admission. This prediction is heavily influenced by your academic standing during law school, where your first and third-year grades placed you in the second decile, significantly below the average of the sixth decile typically seen in successful candidates. Additionally, your LSAT score of 34 and undergraduate GPA of 2.9 are lower than the averages of 37.27 and 3.24 found among those who pass. To help you understand this decision, we looked at "what if" scenarios, which are alternative versions of your profile that would have resulted in an admission approval. These scenarios identify the smallest possible changes to your information that would flip the model’s prediction from a failure to a pass. By comparing your current profile to these successful alternatives, we can pinpoint exactly which factors the model weighed most heavily in your rejection. In our analysis, we generated ten different scenarios where your application would have been accepted, and surprisingly, only one specific factor needed to change across all of them. While your family's upper-middle-income status, your full-time student status, and your LSAT score remained constant, your undergraduate GPA was the sole driver of change in every single successful scenario. Specifically, the model suggests that even a very slight adjustment to your undergraduate GPA—averaging a shift of just 0.1 points—would have been enough to change the outcome. This indicates that your current academic profile sits at a critical threshold where the model is extremely sensitive to your undergraduate performance in relation to your law school deciles. Because your law school decile rankings are currently quite low at 2.0, the model is looking for a specific balance between those grades and your earlier undergraduate work. Since you cannot change your past undergraduate GPA or your LSAT score now, the most realistic path forward involves focusing on the factors that remained fixed in these scenarios but are within your future control. Improving your law school performance from the second decile toward the sixth decile average would drastically shift your probability of success. If you can demonstrate a higher academic standing in your upcoming studies, the model's high certainty of failure would likely collapse, as your current scores are the primary reason for the rejection. Ultimately, the model views your current combination of a 2.9 GPA and low class deciles as a high-risk profile for the bar exam. By focusing on raising your class rank and maintaining your full-time dedication, you can align your profile more closely with the typical successful student. Small shifts in how your academic history is balanced can make the difference between a rejection and an approval in future applications.
